seoTitle: Compassionate Allowance List (2026): 314 Conditions That Fast-Track Disability
seoDescription: Social Security’s Compassionate Allowances list now has 314 conditions. What is on it, how a claim gets flagged, the records that confirm it, why some listed conditions are still denied, the ALS waiting-period waiver, and what a Michigan lawyer does.
tagline: The list decides who is flagged. The records decide who is approved.

c.v: Social Security’s Compassionate Allowances initiative identifies diseases and conditions so serious that, by their nature, they meet the legal definition of disability, and moves claims involving them to the front of the line. A standard disability application in 2026 waits months for an initial decision and a year or more for a hearing. A Compassionate Allowance claim with the right records is often decided in weeks.

on August 11, 2026, when Social Security added 14 more, most of them rare pediatric genetic disorders and aggressive cancers. Since the program began in 2008, more than 1.2 million people have been approved through it. The conditions range from the ones most families would expect, pancreatic cancer, ALS, early-onset Alzheimer’s, glioblastoma, to several hundred rare diseases most people have never heard of.
Two things about the program are misunderstood, and both cost claimants time. First, there is

. You apply for SSDI or SSI the ordinary way, and Social Security’s software flags the claim from what you write. If you describe your condition in words the software does not recognize, the flag is never set. Second, being on the list does not mean

. The claim still has to meet the non-medical requirements for the program you applied for, and the medical records still have to confirm the diagnosis at the stage or severity the list specifies. A claim for “metastatic breast cancer” without a pathology report or imaging confirming metastasis is a standard claim, not a Compassionate Allowance.

This page explains what is on the list and how it is organized, how a claim is flagged and decided, what records each kind of condition requires, the waiting period and the ALS exception, the other fast tracks, what happens when a listed condition is denied anyway, and what a Michigan disability lawyer does in a case that should move quickly.

sections.heading: Why a listed condition is still sometimes denied

c.v: Compassionate Allowance claims are denied for the same reasons as other claims, and the speed of the process can make the reasons harder to see.
The non-medical requirements were not met.

items.v: For SSDI, you must be insured: enough recent work credits. For SSI, your income and resources must be under the limits ($2,000 in countable resources for an individual in 2026). A Compassionate Allowance condition does not change those rules; a claimant who has not worked in a decade and owns a second vehicle may be denied both programs with a diagnosis that is plainly on the list. sections.heading: The waiting period, back pay, and the ALS exception

items.v: pays nothing for the first five full calendar months after the onset of disability; the first payment is for the sixth month. If your condition was diagnosed and you stopped working six or more months before you applied, the waiting period has already run and benefits begin immediately on approval, with retroactive pay for up to 12 months before the application date.

Under the ALS Disability Insurance Access Act, as amended, qualifying SSDI claims based on ALS are exempt from the five-month waiting period, including claims approved on or after July 23, 2020. Eligible SSDI beneficiaries with ALS also do not have the usual 24-month Medicare waiting period.

sections.heading: If the claimant dies before the decision

c.v: Many Compassionate Allowance conditions are terminal, and some claimants die while the claim is pending. The claim may still be processed to determine whether benefits were owed before death. For SSDI, unpaid benefits may be payable to eligible surviving family members or, in certain circumstances, the estate’s legal representative, under 20 CFR 404.503. SSI has different and more restrictive rules under 20 CFR 416.542, and unpaid SSI benefits generally cannot be paid to the estate. A spouse or dependent child may also qualify separately for Social Security survivors’ benefits. Notify Social Security promptly, because continuing the claim and obtaining any unpaid benefits depends on the applicable eligibility and payment rules.

faqs.question: Is there a separate application for a Compassionate Allowance?

answer.v: No. You apply for SSDI or SSI in the ordinary way, online, by phone at 1-800-772-1213, or at a field office. Social Security’s software flags the claim from the condition you describe. Our

faqs.question: How many conditions are on the list?

answer.v: 314, as of August 11, 2026, when 14 were added. The list is at ssa.gov/compassionateallowances/conditions.htm and changes each year.

faqs.question: My condition is on the list. Am I automatically approved?

answer.v: No. You must still meet the non-medical requirements (work credits for SSDI, income and resource limits for SSI), be earning less than the substantial gainful activity limit ($1,690 a month in 2026), and have records that confirm the diagnosis at the stage or severity the list specifies.

faqs.question: How long does a Compassionate Allowance claim take?

answer.v: Social Security does not publish an average. Claims with the diagnosis named correctly and confirming records attached are commonly decided in weeks rather than months. Claims where the examiner must chase records take longer.

faqs.question: Does a Compassionate Allowance eliminate the five-month waiting period?

answer.v: No, except for ALS. For every other condition, SSDI pays beginning with the sixth full month after onset. If your onset was more than five months before you applied, the wait has already run.

faqs.question: I have stage II cancer. Is that a Compassionate Allowance?

answer.v: Usually not; most cancers are listed only at advanced or metastatic stages, or as specific aggressive types. A stage II cancer may still qualify under the cancer Listings or the five-step test, and the claim should be filed either way.

faqs.question: My condition is not on the list but is just as serious. What do I do?

answer.v: Apply. The list is a fast track, not the only road. Your condition may meet a Listing or prevent all work, and if it is terminal it may be flagged TERI regardless of the list. Social Security also accepts public suggestions for conditions to add.

faqs.question: Can I get SSI payments before the decision?

answer.v: For certain conditions, yes: presumptive disability payments for up to six months under 20 CFR 416.934, including for ALS, terminal illness with hospice confirmation, and others. The field office makes the determination at filing.

faqs.question: What happens to the claim if my family member dies before it is decided?

answer.v: The claim continues. A surviving spouse, child, parent, or the estate can be substituted and paid the benefits due through the month of death, and survivors’ benefits may be available. Notify Social Security and ask for substitution; it is not automatic.
